openings.text: On the sunny rooftop, Mina wanted a graceful kite flight, Pip wanted a daring dragon flourish, and Tavi wanted to be included in a surprise. Then Mina opened the little wooden tube.
Bright scraps waited beside the paper kite while three friends imagined three different kinds of hello. Mina lifted the tube’s lid to find out what the kite would carry.

variants.text: Mina opened the wooden tube and read the label aloud. “This hello is for {phrase:tube.label}!” she said, blinking at the unexpected name.
Mina found Pip beside the worktable. “The tube says {phrase:tube.label},” she told him. Pip’s little smoke-puff curled into a question mark.
Tavi leaned close, still guarding the secret in his enormous imagination. Mina showed him the label: “It says {phrase:tube.label}, not a birthday surprise.”
Tavi puffed out his cheeks. “A birthday surprise needs a huge audience!” he announced, accidentally telling everyone that he had been planning something enormous.
When Tavi saw the words {phrase:tube.label}, his grand secret shrank into a sheepish smile. “Oh,” he said. “Then the birds should get the first hello.”
Mina placed the tube in Pip’s careful claws. “Keep it safe and keep the flight gentle.” Pip tucked it close, as if it were a sleeping beetle.
Mina handed Tavi the tube. Tavi held it with both hands and nodded solemnly. “No giant birthday announcement,” he promised. “Only the right kind of hello.”
Mina passed Tavi the brass bell, and he gave it one tiny test jingle.
Tavi tied the bell beneath the kite’s nose. Its {phrase:bell.tone} note made the paper wings shiver with excitement.
Mina chose the {phrase:scraps.color} scrap and fastened it into a long tail. “A steady tail for a steady hello,” she said.
Before Mina could say “perhaps not,” Pip clipped on a dragon fin. The kite suddenly looked ready to sneeze fire and chase the moon.
Pip glanced at the tube, then at Mina’s careful tail. “I can fly quietly,” he said. “Quietly can still be splendid.” His smoke puff became a tiny silver star.
“No roaring dragon tricks?” Pip asked. Mina shook her head. Pip sighed theatrically, then smiled. “Very well. I shall be the world’s gentlest dragon messenger.”
Mina studied the proud fin. Pip held his breath. At last Mina gave one careful nod. “One dragon flourish.” Pip’s grin grew so wide that a smoke ring escaped.
“If the kite is going to be a dragon,” Mina said, “let it be a magnificent one.” Pip bowed to the paper wings, which immediately wobbled like dancing noodles.
The kite rose in a calm little arc. Pip held the tube close while Mina guided the string, and the paper tail traced a neat blue-gold-red smile across the sky.
The kite lifted above the garden. Its bell rang a bright or low little song, and Tavi waved the tube as proudly as a tiny parade marshal.
The fin caught the air. The kite swooped left, looped right, and performed a dragon dance so grand that Pip nearly applauded himself.
Pip added one neat smoke ring, shaped like a surprised dragon wearing a crown.
Mina ran three steps and released the kite. Up it climbed, tugging the spool toward the bright blue sky.
The smooth kite settled beside Grandma, its paper tail fluttering like a tiny flag. Pip’s quiet hello had arrived without waking a single sleeping pigeon.
The bell rang over the garden, and the birds answered with a ridiculous chorus: cheep-cheep, squawk, and one very serious “boing!”
The message arrived beneath Pip’s smoky dragon shadow. The kite looped once more, as if the clouds themselves had requested an encore.
Pip’s fin flashed against the sun, and the cloud dragon received its message under a grand, wiggly dragon silhouette.

endings.text: The kite rested beside Grandma, its tail whispering against the rooftop while Pip’s careful claws held the empty string.
Far below, Grandma waved. Above her, the kite’s little paper tail made one graceful bow.
The garden birds answered the ringing bell with a chorus so silly that Tavi laughed until he had to sit on the worktable.
The brass bell kept jingling over the garden, while three birds hopped in a row as if they were applauding with their feet.
Pip’s fin caught the sun, the kite looped beneath its smoky dragon shadow, and the cloud dragon’s hello sailed into the blue.
The kite danced a dragon’s wobbly victory above the roof. Pip bowed so deeply that his last smoke ring landed on his own nose.
Tavi stood beside Mina and Pip, all three shadows holding one string while the message glided toward the garden birds.
Three shadows stretched across the roof—one careful, one scaly, one small—as the kite carried its true hello away.
